name: Rapamycin
summary: An immune-suppressing transplant drug (sirolimus) that extends lifespan in mice and is being studied in people as a possible way to slow aging.
what_it_is: Rapamycin, also called sirolimus and sold as Rapamune, is a prescription drug that suppresses the immune system. It blocks a signaling pathway called mTOR, which mouse studies have linked to lifespan. It is approved to prevent kidney transplant rejection and to treat lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), a rare lung disease, and it is being tested in small human trials for aging.

evidence.why: It is an approved transplant and LAM drug, but for aging the evidence is mouse lifespan studies plus small, short human trials of aging markers rather than lifespan or disease outcomes.

status_us.label: FDA-approved transplant and LAM drug; not for aging
status_us.note: Rapamune is approved to prevent organ rejection in kidney transplant patients aged 13 and older and to treat LAM, with a boxed warning about immunosuppression, infections and cancer. It is not approved for aging, and the label says only physicians experienced in immunosuppressive therapy should prescribe it for transplant patients.

benefits.claim: Prevents organ rejection in kidney transplant patients aged 13 and older (approved use)
Treats lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), a rare lung disease (approved use)
Longer lifespan in genetically diverse mice, even when started late in life: 14% for females and 9% for males at the age when 90% had died, at three test sites
Improved some aging-related measures of the immune system, heart and blood vessels, and skin in a review of 19 human studies, but not muscle, hormone or nervous-system measures
No change in visceral fat (the main outcome) in a 48-week trial of 114 healthy adults aged 50 to 85; women on the higher dose gained lean tissue and reported less pain

risks.risk: Boxed warning: a weakened immune system raises the risk of infections and of lymphoma and other cancers; not recommended after liver or lung transplant because of excess deaths, graft loss and other serious complications
High cholesterol and triglycerides, swelling (edema) and high blood pressure, each in 30% or more of kidney transplant patients
Mouth sores, diarrhea, nausea, acne and headache, each in 20% or more of LAM patients
Slow wound healing, lung inflammation (interstitial lung disease, sometimes fatal), protein in the urine and skin cancer
Angioedema (swelling of the face, lips or throat), more likely when taken with other drugs that can cause it, such as ACE inhibitors
High blood sugar and new diabetes have been reported
Harm to a developing baby, and low or absent sperm counts
In healthy older adults on the regimen tested, more stomach and gut complaints than placebo (about 1 in 5 versus 1 in 10), with similar rates of serious events

avoid_if: Pregnant or planning pregnancy (it can harm a fetus; the label advises highly effective contraception during treatment and for 12 weeks after)
Liver or lung transplant recipients (not recommended)
Active infection or a weakened immune system
Planning to get a live vaccine (live vaccines should be avoided during treatment)
interactions: Strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors such as ketoconazole, voriconazole, itraconazole, erythromycin and clarithromycin: avoid, as they raise sirolimus levels
Strong CYP3A4/P-gp inducers such as rifampin and rifabutin: avoid, as they lower sirolimus levels
ACE inhibitors: raise the risk of angioedema
Grapefruit juice: must not be taken with it
Cyclosporine: interacts with sirolimus, and the label sets rules for using them together

labs.why: The label recommends sirolimus level checks, lipid monitoring and periodic urine-protein and kidney tests; these were set for transplant and LAM care, and no monitoring plan has been established for use in aging.

studies.title: Targeting ageing with rapamycin and its derivatives in humans: a systematic review
studies.people: 19 studies in healthy adults and people with aging-related diseases
studies.finding: Rapamycin and related drugs improved some immune, cardiovascular and skin measures but not endocrine, muscle or nervous-system measures; healthy people had no serious drug-related events, while patients had more infections and higher cholesterol and triglycerides.

studies.title: Influence of rapamycin on safety and healthspan metrics after one year: PEARL trial results
studies.finding: Low-dose intermittent rapamycin did not change visceral fat; women on the higher dose gained lean tissue and had less pain, and adverse events were similar to placebo. The trial was small and several authors work for the company that ran it.

studies.title: Rapamycin fed late in life extends lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice
studies.people: Genetically diverse mice at three test sites
studies.finding: Rapamycin started at 600 days of age extended median and maximal lifespan in both sexes, possibly by delaying cancer deaths, slowing aging, or both.

ask_your_clinician: Given my infection history, cholesterol and any planned surgery, what are the risks of rapamycin for me?
Which of my medicines, supplements or foods could change rapamycin levels?
Is there a clinical trial of rapamycin for aging that I could join?

notes_for_editor: Human aging evidence is thin: the systematic review mixed populations and drugs (it includes related drugs such as everolimus), and PEARL was small, enrolled few women, used compounded rapamycin later found to give lower blood levels than commercial tablets, and was run by a company with a commercial interest. The Pfizer label (revised October 2024) was read up to the kidney-transplant trials; the LAM trial results could not be retrieved, so LAM is stated only as an approved indication. Most side-effect frequencies come from transplant and LAM patients taking it daily, often with other immunosuppressants; risks at the intermittent doses used for aging are less known. 'Active infection or a weakened immune system' in avoid_if is inferred from the boxed warning.
